extracted.intended_audience: physicians, medical researchers, social-science readers, and educated general readers (delegates to medical congress / subscribers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the evaluative criteria and normative claims used in a Victorian-era Popular Science Monthly essay about the 'militant' type of society and an opening address on the cultivation of medical science. Focuses on the traits a society must have to succeed at war and the qualities required for scientific progress in medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily vigor and courage as determinants of war success
rubrics_metrics.description: Other things equal, a society will be successful in war in proportion as its members are endowed with bodily vigor and courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Egyptian and Assyrian sculptures and inscriptions as evidence that prowess was most honored; asserts that among conflicting societies those with marked physical and mental powers required in battle survive and spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of virtue with bravery / honor of prowess
rubrics_metrics.description: In militant societies virtue is identified with bravery and strength; goodness is equated with the strong and daring rather than moral sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and historical examples: Grote on ancient Greeks, Roman identification of virtue with bravery, the knightly character in medieval Europe where fearless-ness made other qualities acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenge as duty; lex talionis internalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaliation and the lex talionis become normative rules; failure to revenge is regarded as a disgrace and revenge becomes a private and public duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Feejeeans fostering anger in children, Japanese customs about the slayer of kin, medieval France and the Abbe Brantome's statement about revenge; Montenegro practices and Boue's quote showing the moral obligation to acquire a 'head' in vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight in destruction and disregard for life
rubrics_metrics.description: Where destruction of enemies is chronic, destruction becomes a source of pleasure and there is a cultural applause for ferocity and bloodshed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence given: Dahoman annual customs with public slaughter, Feejeeans cannibal feasts and infant destruction, Mongol and Turkish mass violence, Spartan massacre of Helots, Roman emperors' murders and arena spectacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low regard for liberty (readiness to enslave and restrain)
rubrics_metrics.description: In militant regimes there is little regard for liberty; captives are enslaved and the freedom of individuals is readily curtailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author links contempt for life with contempt for liberty; militant savages enslaving captives is cited as habitual; primitive Christianity did not expressly condemn slavery, showing the depth of the sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard for property; plunder and appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of property by weaker members are little respected where mastery by force is honorable; plunder, appropriation, and theft may be considered virtuous if undiscovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Feejee chiefs seizing subjects' goods; Dahomey king 'squeezing' those who acquire property; Spartan applause for pilferers; Merovingian and Charlemagne-era plunder by officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt for manual labor and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: In militant societies labor (especially manual work and trade) is scorned and regarded as dishonorable, often associated with slaves or low origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dahomey despising agriculture because slaves work it; Japanese nobles' contempt for traffic; Wilkinson on Egyptian prejudices against mechanical employments; Persians’ contempt for trade and Roman proscriptions against senators engaging in speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriotism as a motivator for risking life
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentiment of patriotism (belief that it is glorious to die for one's country) greatly conduces to success in war, though mercenaries can fight without it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes patriotism is not strictly essential but is strongly advantageous; absence of patriotism is unfavorable to offensive and defensive action and can lead to failure and subjugation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct of obedience and loyalty to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful militant societies require readiness of individuals to subordinate their wills to a commander or ruler; loyalty and obedience are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Araucanians' temporary obedience in wartime, Feejeeans' intense loyalty (sacrificial burials), ancient Egypt's 'blind obedience', Sparta's profound obedience to political agencies, primitive Rome's submission to appointed leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited faith in governmental agency / officialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Militant regimes foster belief that public agencies should control all affairs; generations raised under such systems tacitly assume matters can only be thus controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites ancient Peru where regimental rule left no materials for industrial thought; modern examples include expansion of state functions and desiring fewer witnesses at executions—signs of freeing officialism from popular checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repression of individual initiative and lack of private enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive regimentation reduces independent action—slaves do only what they are told; masters require permission for unusual acts—producing passive acceptance and expectancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: mental state of passive acceptance, dependency on public agencies for all spheres of life, erosion of private prompting ideas and sentiments that might create other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal-causation worldview that impedes scientific thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Militant societies emphasize personal agency (commanders and rulers) and thereby inhibit the development of impersonal causal explanations and scientific understanding of natural and social processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues sciences grow from arts and recognition of uniformities; continual experience of personal agency (army, official control) makes history read as doings of remarkable men and prevents conceiving self-regulating social processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual repression and contempt for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Warlike activities lead to contempt for intellectual culture and retard emancipation from primitive ideas; knowledge acquisition is scorned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Spartans scorned learning; in medieval Europe learning was derided as for clerks and people of mean origin; militancy is antagonistic to science and industrial progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid hierarchical organization and compulsory cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: To marshal combined efforts for war, societies develop descending grades of command, centralized authority, and compulsory cooperation that decrease social mobility and flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural elements: universal service of individuals to society, sub-centers through which orders are conveyed, negative and positive regulation (restraining and directing citizens), and increasing rigidity with development of militant type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of executive/regulatory functions and removal of popular checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Militant tendencies produce extensions of public agency, central inspection, compulsory schemes (e.g., insurance), and efforts to free officialism from popular oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete instances: regulation by policemen (Birmingham, London), Cyprus business and Indian Viceroy acting under secret instructions, proposals for registration of teachers and central inspection of libraries, the bill for compulsory insurance cited as example of regulatory policy extending itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molding of citizens morally and intellectually into a militant-adapted form
rubrics_metrics.description: Militant social structures shape citizens to identify goodness with strength, to accept revenge and sacrifice of others, to show deadened sympathies, high loyalty, faith, obedience, and low initiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary statement tying earlier traits together: patriotism, loyalty, obedience, faith in authority, little power of initiation, habit of seeing official control everywhere, and inability to conceive self-regulating arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of minds fosters medical and scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: A diversity of national characters, ages, theoretical and practical temperaments, and educations is valuable and representative for the cultivation of medical science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the opening address Sir James Paget praises the international congress composition (elder and younger men, thoughtful and practical, men of fact and imagination) as offering wide opportunities for research and mutual improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicine offers vast opportunities for original research
rubrics_metrics.description: Because human life is complex and presented in infinite multiformity (ages, occupations, climates, social states), medicine is 'preeminent in its range of opportunities for scientific study.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Every condition of life presents different problems; wherever duty or curiosity leads there are materials and opportunities for separate original research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate selection and structuring of subjects for productive discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: A congress should not leave work to chance or to sentiment; certain subjects should be selected and arranged into sections for focused discussion and progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paget argues chosen subjects (by custom of former meetings) are the most stirring and practical questions that can benefit from wide discussion; sections and presidents will lead these discussions rather than random chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for collection of well-observed facts by many observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scientific questions chiefly need the collection of facts well observed by many persons; agreement of many minds helps counteract the personal element in observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author: 'things are not what they appear to each one mind'—to attain certainty even on matters of fact many observers are needed so personal elements are counteracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of doubt, debate, and even error in arriving at truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubts, contrary pleadings, and even error may be useful in a congress as they can help bring out truth and make it express its whole strength and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paget allows that while a prevalence of errors is not desirable, error's exposure in discussion serves to clarify and strengthen truth; 'adversity is an excellent school for truth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental pliancy and readiness for variation required for scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Minds must be pliant and quick to adjust to new knowledge or methods; for progressive science there must be minds that remain 'young' in their adaptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author stresses that advances change the circumstances of mental life and that minds unable or unwilling to adjust become less useful; the congress illustrates and promotes such pliancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific advances demand adaptation to new methods and senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Major advances (e.g., auscultation, numerical methods, acceptance of evolution) require refinement of senses, new recording and thinking methods, and adjustment in mental habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show that discovery of auscultation required refined hearing; numerical methods required recording and thinking in new ways; evolutionary doctrine changed whole departments of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-adjustment and population diversity promote long-term scientific and social prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as species that self-adjust thrive, races of men whose minds self-adjust to new conditions and produce diverse populations adapted to varied circumstances are most prosperous in high civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with biology: self-adjustment to varying conditions produces strength; those adapted to products of their arts prosper most and increase science's possessions and applications.
